chapter.title: Collections
chapter.para: .NET's collections are typed, and keep their own indexing: a list counts from 0, a dictionary goes by key. Its arrays are the exception: they count from 1, as Rexx Arrays.

section.title: Lists
section.para: You want a growable list, sorted by .NET or by your own rule.

example.title: Lists
example.programlisting:
names = .net~type("System.Collections.Generic.List<string>")~new do n over "pear fig apple banana"~makeArray(" "); names~Add(n); end names~Sort say names~Count names[0] names~Contains("fig") names~IndexOf("pear") names~Sort(.net~handler(.ByLength~new, "COMPARE")) say names~ToArray~makeString("L", " ") names~RemoveAt(0); names~Insert(0, "kiwi") do with index i item n over names; say i n; end
::requires "net.cls" ::class ByLength ::method compare use arg a, b return a~length - b~length
example.screen: 4 apple 1 3 fig pear apple banana 0 kiwi 1 pear 2 apple 3 banana

section.para: How it works. .net~type("System.Collections.Generic.List<string>") names a generic type in C# syntax. A list counts from 0 (names[0], IndexOf, RemoveAt), as .NET documents it, and DO WITH INDEX gives those positions. Sort without arguments uses the items' own order; with a handler, a Rexx method compares two items, as a Comparison<string>, and returns a negative number, zero, or a positive one.
See also Reference, Arrays, Collections and References, Callbacks, Events and Tasks.

section.title: Dictionaries
section.para: You want to count, or to look things up by key.

example.title: Dictionaries
example.programlisting:
count = .net~type("System.Collections.Generic.Dictionary<string, int>")~new text = "the cat and the dog and the bird" do w over text~makeArray(" ") r = .net~ref if count~TryGetValue(w, r) then count[w] = r~value + 1 else count[w] = 1 end do with index word item n over count; say word n; end say count~ContainsKey("cat") count~Count sorted = .net~type("System.Collections.Generic.SortedDictionary<string, int>")~new(count) say sorted~Keys~makeArray~makeString("L", " ")
::requires "net.cls"
example.screen: the 3 cat 1 and 2 dog 1 bird 1 1 5 and bird cat dog the

section.para: How it works. A Dictionary<string, int> is indexed by key: count[w] = 1. TryGetValue has an out parameter, which takes a NetRef (.net~ref): after the call, its value is what the method put there. DO WITH INDEX k ITEM v gives keys and values. A SortedDictionary made from it keeps its keys in order.
See also Reference, Arrays, Collections and References.

section.title: LINQ Queries
section.para: You want to filter, transform, sort and sum sequences, as LINQ does.

example.title: LINQ Queries
example.programlisting:
e = .net~System~Linq~Enumerable nums = e~Range(1, 10) evens = e~Where(nums, .net~handler(.Q~new, "EVEN")) squares = .net~invoke(e, "Select<int, int>", evens, .net~handler(.Q~new, "SQUARE")) say e~ToArray(squares)~makeString("L", " ") say e~Sum(squares) e~Count(evens) e~Max(nums) e~Average(nums) words = .array~of("pear", "fig", "apple") byLength = .net~invoke(e, "OrderBy<string, int>", words, .net~handler(.Q~new, "LEN")) say e~ToArray(byLength)~makeString("L", " ")
::requires "net.cls" ::class Q ::method even use arg n return n // 2 = 0 ::method square use arg n return n * n ::method len use arg s return s~length

section.para: How it works. LINQ's methods are static methods of Enumerable, called as such: e~Where(seq, predicate), not seq~Where(...). A handler is the lambda: a Rexx method that gets an item and returns the answer. Where's type argument is inferred from the sequence; Select and OrderBy also need the type that the lambda returns, which a Rexx method does not declare: they are given in the name, .net~invoke(e, "Select<int, int>", ...). A Rexx Array is a sequence too.
See also Reference, Names and Messages, Callbacks, Events and Tasks.

section.title: Sets, Queues, Stacks
section.para: You want a set, a queue, a stack or a priority queue.

example.title: Sets, Queues, Stacks
example.programlisting:
set = .net~type("System.Collections.Generic.HashSet<string>")~new say set~Add("a") set~Add("b") set~Add("a") set~Count q = .net~type("System.Collections.Generic.Queue<int>")~new q~Enqueue(1); q~Enqueue(2); q~Enqueue(3) say q~Dequeue q~Peek q~Count st = .net~type("System.Collections.Generic.Stack<string>")~new st~Push("x"); st~Push("y") say st~Pop st~Count pq = .net~type("System.Collections.Generic.PriorityQueue<string, int>")~new pq~Enqueue("low", 9); pq~Enqueue("high", 1); pq~Enqueue("mid", 5) do while pq~Count > 0; say pq~Dequeue; end
::requires "net.cls"

section.para: How it works. Each is a generic type, made as any other. set~Add(x) answers whether it was added, as a Rexx logical value. A PriorityQueue<string, int> gives its items in the order of their priorities.
See also Reference, Arrays, Collections and References.
